source.title: GraphFM: A generalist graph transformer that learns transferable representations across diverse domains
source.authors: Divyansha Lachi; Mehdi Azabou; Vinam Arora; Eva L. Dyer

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some appendix tables are flattened in the extraction, but the relevant scaling results are described in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports graph-model scaling and downstream accuracy results, but does not test the language-model loss laws or compute-optimal allocation in the claim versions. Its references to language-model scaling are background motivation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports graph-model downstream accuracy while varying model size, pretraining tokens, and data composition. These are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"] because they concern graph models and accuracy, not the language-model losses or allocation named in the versions. Values used only to define settings or select hyperparameters are not recorded as outcomes.
record.test_reason: The study cites Kaplan et al. only as motivation. Its own scaling results are graph-transformer downstream node-classification accuracies at three configurations, and model size and token count change together. No loss is measured and no power law is fitted, so no version is tested. V5 needs a power-law form in another modality, and three confounded accuracy points cannot show one. V6 concerns language models.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that larger models trained on more and more diverse graph data generalize better to unseen graphs, and that adding biological and synthetic graphs helps. They call diversity a key driver, and say repeatable scaling laws for graphs remain future work.
record.recipe_differences: The study scales graph-model pretraining and evaluates downstream graph classification accuracy; it does not use the language-model held-out cross-entropy measurements or compute-optimal allocation procedure in the original scaling-law studies.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported scaling results vary with pretraining data composition; adding biological and then synthetic graphs is associated with successive increases in mean accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: GraphFM mean MFT accuracy on 9 held-out graph datasets rises monotonically across 389K/200K, 18M/2M and 75M/7.3M (params/tokens) configurations. The largest gives +2.1%, with larger gains on harder datasets.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In multi-graph pretraining, jointly scaling model size and pretraining tokens improves downstream node-classification accuracy on unseen graphs.

fits_no_version.finding: Mean accuracy rises from 0.714 (Soc) to 0.722 (Soc+Bio), 0.735 (all real) and 0.750 (all plus synthetic).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adding diverse, including synthetic, pretraining graphs improves graph-model transfer accuracy.

record.problems: The scaling comparison changes model size and pretraining token count together, so their separate contributions are not isolated in the main three-configuration result. The reported mean accuracy values for those configurations are not stated in the text, and the reported graph-scaling accuracy results do not establish language-model loss laws.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results were left out. The text describes dataset-level scaling patterns in Figure A5 but does not provide numerical values for those individual curves in the text.

untested.parts: Not tested: held-out pretraining loss and power-law fits in parameters, tokens or compute.
Not tested: extrapolation from fitted small-run laws.
Not tested: compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Size and data are varied jointly.
Not tested: depth and width effects at a fixed parameter count. Configurations differ in size.
Not tested: whether a power-law form holds for graph models. Only three accuracy points, with no fit and no loss.
Not tested: language-model downstream predictability. The graph accuracy trend is not fitted or predicted.
Not tested: dependence of exponents or allocation on fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: Kaplan et al. 2020 is cited only as motivation. The three-point scaling confounds parameters and tokens, measures accuracy rather than loss, and fits no functional form. The domain-composition runs also confound token count with diversity.

versions.untested_parts: Not tested: language-model held-out cross-entropy power laws over parameters, tokens, or compute.
Not tested: prediction of much larger language-model runs from power-law fits on smaller runs.
Not tested: loss-minimising language-model parameter/token allocations at fixed compute or their scaling with compute.
Not tested: effects of depth, width, or other architecture details on language-model loss at fixed parameter count.
The study concerns graph models, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds for held-out loss in another modality or training regime.
The study measures downstream accuracy for graph models, not language-model downstream performance or its predictability from pretraining loss or scale.
Not tested: dependence of language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations on setup and fitting choices, or departures from a single power law.

rows.operation_detail: Increased model size and pretraining token count across three configurations

conditions.value: MFT; mean accuracy across held-out test datasets

rows.measure: Mean downstream accuracy across held-out graph datasets
rows.value: Performance improved consistently as data size increased; the largest model trained on 7.3M tokens achieved a 2.1% increase in accuracy compared to the smaller models.
rows.note: Aggregate result across the three model/data-scale configurations; the text does not give the exact mean accuracy values for each configuration.
rows.check: Monotone accuracy gain (about 2.1%) across three configurations that change parameters and tokens together. Per-configuration values are not given in the text, and no functional form is fitted. This is a related finding, not a version test.
